Read the story and answer questions 7 to 12.

Sopaipillas for Multicultural Day

When Ms. Patel announced Multicultural Day, everyone in Grade 5 had to bring a dish from their family's country. Josefina's stomach dropped. She had moved from Santiago to Ottawa the year before, and she still felt like a visitor in her own class.

"Sopaipillas," her father said that night, without looking up from his laptop. "Your abuela's recipe. Pumpkin, flour, a little butter. Fried. Easy."

It was not easy. On Saturday, Josefina's first batch came out flat and grey. The second batch stuck to the pan. By the third batch, the kitchen smelled of burnt oil, and her father had quietly opened every window in the apartment.

"Maybe I should just bring cookies from the store," she said.

Her father closed his laptop. He got up, washed his hands, and made a video call to Santiago. Abuela appeared on the screen in her apron. "The pumpkin is too wet," she said after one look. "Squeeze it. And the oil has to be hotter than you think."

The fourth batch puffed up golden and round. Josefina ate one standing at the stove. It tasted like her grandmother's kitchen.

On Monday, she put the plate on the long table between a Lebanese salad and a tray of Jamaican patties. A boy named Theo took one, then another, then came back with three friends. By lunch, the plate was empty, and Josefina had explained the word "sopaipilla" eleven times.

That night, she wrote Abuela a message: "They loved them. Next year I'm making them for the whole school."

Read the text and answer questions 13 to 18.

Monarch Butterflies: The Longest Journey

A tiny traveler. Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave Canada and the northern United States and fly south to the mountains of central Mexico. The trip can be 4,000 kilometers long. A monarch weighs less than a gram, about the same as a paper clip, yet it crosses lakes, cities and deserts to reach a forest it has never seen.

One plant. A monarch caterpillar eats only one plant: milkweed. Milkweed contains a poison that does not harm the caterpillar but stays in its body. When the caterpillar becomes a butterfly, that poison makes it taste terrible to birds. The monarch's bright orange wings are a warning: "Don't eat me."

The super generation. Most monarchs live only a few weeks. But the butterflies born at the end of summer are different. This "super generation" lives up to eight months, long enough to fly to Mexico, spend the winter hanging in huge clusters on fir trees, and start the trip back in spring. Their grandchildren and great-grandchildren complete the journey north.

Fewer every year. Scientists have counted far fewer monarchs in recent years. Farmers have removed milkweed from their fields with chemicals, so caterpillars have less to eat. In Mexico, some of the winter forests have been cut down. To help, thousands of people in Canada, the United States and Mexico now plant milkweed in gardens and along roads, creating a chain of small "butterfly stations" for the long trip.

First Snow

The first snow falls like feathers from a pillow torn in two,
It tucks the sleeping garden in and hides the path from view.
The fence wears a white sweater, the mailbox wears a hat,
The pine trees stand like soldiers where the summer swallows sat.
My boots are the first to write on this clean white page,
Each step a word, each path a line, the whole yard is my stage.
By noon the sun will read it all and wipe the page away,
So I'll write the longest story that I can write today.

pauta.respuesta: B) A simile

Guion de Listening (leer dos veces, en voz alta)

Lee a ritmo normal. Pausa de 30 segundos entre lecturas. No expliques palabras ni respondas preguntas sobre el contenido.

The Night the Power Went Out

On the last Sunday of July, the wind in Temuco blew so hard that the lights went out at seven in the evening. Valentina's whole house went dark and silent. No television, no internet, no music. Her little brother Benjamín started to cry.

"Don't worry," said their mother. She found a box of candles in the kitchen and lit four of them on the table. Their father took the big pot and made popcorn on the gas stove, because the gas still worked.

Then Grandpa did something nobody expected. He sat in his chair, closed his eyes, and began to tell a story about the time he got lost in the mountains when he was twelve. He talked for almost an hour. Nobody moved. Benjamín stopped crying and sat on the floor with his mouth open.

When the lights came back at nine o'clock, Valentina surprised everyone. She stood up and turned them off again. "Grandpa hasn't finished," she said.

The next day, Valentina's father bought a box of candles. He put it in the kitchen, not for the next storm, but for the next Sunday.

Guion de Speaking (5 minutos)

Solo en inglés. Tres tareas de ~1,5 minutos. No corrijas durante la conversación; anota y califica al final con la rúbrica.

  1. Warm-up (20 s, no se califica): "Hi! What are you going to do this summer?"
  2. Opinion: "Some people think children should not use screens (TV, tablets, phones) during the week. Do you agree? Give me two reasons, and tell me what someone who disagrees might say." Apoyo: "Can you give me an example?"
  3. Process: "Explain to me, step by step, how to prepare your favorite breakfast, or how to prepare for a test." Apoyo: "What do you need?" / "What comes next?" / "What is the last step?"
  4. Story: "Tell me about a time something went wrong and it ended up being a good day anyway. Beginning, middle and end." Apoyo: "What happened first?" / "How did it end?" / "How did you feel?"
  5. Cierre: "Thank you, that's all. Well done."

Rúbricas

Escritura (ítem 30) — 5 criterios, cada uno 0, 1 o 2 puntos (máximo 10). Es la rúbrica DIA de escritura adaptada:

Criterio 2 pts 1 pt 0 pts
Propósito y estructura Opción A: inicio, medio (problema) y final (solución) claros, con al menos una línea de diálogo bien puntuada. Opción B: afirmación, dos razones, contraargumento con respuesta y conclusión Falta una parte (p. ej. sin final claro; sin contraargumento) Falta más de una parte o no cumple la tarea
Coherencia y conectores Las ideas siguen un orden lógico y usa conectores variados (first, then, suddenly, because, however, finally) Orden mayormente claro pero conectores escasos o repetidos Ideas desordenadas o inconexas
Desarrollo de ideas Detalles concretos (qué pasó exactamente, ejemplos para cada razón); 10-12 líneas Ideas correctas pero poco desarrolladas o texto corto (7-9 líneas) Ideas muy generales o texto muy breve (menos de 7 líneas)
Vocabulario Palabras precisas y variadas para la edad; palabras de sentimiento o de opinión Vocabulario correcto pero básico y repetitivo Vocabulario muy limitado o con palabras en español
Ortografía, gramática y puntuación Mayúsculas, puntos, apóstrofes y comillas correctos; tiempos verbales consistentes; máximo 3 errores en total 4-6 errores que no impiden entender Más de 6 errores o errores que dificultan entender

Speaking (ítem 31) — cada criterio 0, 1 o 2 puntos:

Criterio 2 pts 1 pt 0 pts
Contenido Cumple las tres tareas: opinión con 2 razones y contraargumento, proceso completo, historia con sus tres partes Dos tareas completas o las tres incompletas Una tarea o menos
Organización Ideas en orden con conectores variados (first, then, because, however, finally, in the end) Orden confuso o conectores repetitivos Sin estructura
Vocabulario Rico y preciso; expresiones de opinión y contraste; sin recurrir al español Repite palabras básicas o cambia a español en 1-2 palabras Muy limitado; mezcla español con frecuencia
Corrección Tiempos verbales variados (pasado, presente perfecto, would) y concordancia correctos casi siempre (máximo 2 errores) Varios errores que no impiden entender Errores constantes

Qué mira este instrumento

Examen acumulativo del año (fases A, B y C). Muestrea todos los dominios: comprensión auditiva narrativa con inferencia (1-6); narración con preguntas literales, de secuencia, rasgo de personaje, inferencia y cambio del personaje con evidencia (7-12, RL.5.1-RL.5.3); texto informativo con idea principal, características del texto, causa-efecto, estructura, vocabulario en contexto y dos ideas principales (13-18, RI.5.2-RI.5.5); poema con símil, metáfora, rima e inferencia (19-22, RL.5.4); gramática y vocabulario de las cinco semanas (23-29); escritura extensa con rúbrica de 5 criterios (30); speaking con tres tareas (31).

Cómo leerlo: separa el puntaje en tres bloques. Comprensión (1-22, 32 pts): si está sobre 80%, el niño lee y escucha en inglés al nivel de un nativo de Grade 5. Forma escrita (23-29 y criterio de ortografía del 30, 9 pts): si está bajo 60% con buena comprensión, el diagnóstico es claro: sabe el idioma pero no sus convenciones escritas, que se aprenden en pocos meses con práctica dirigida. Producción (30-31, 18 pts): mira los criterios, no el total; "estructura" y "desarrollo" son pensamiento y se trabajan también en español; "ortografía" y "corrección" son forma.

Si le fue mal

  • Comprensión bajo 60%: volver a las guías S1 y S2 (narración e informativo) con lectura diaria de 15 minutos en inglés y una pregunta de inferencia por día ("how do you know?").
  • Forma escrita bajo 60%: una semana por tema con las cajas de gramática de las guías: pasado irregular → plurales → comparativos → presente perfecto → puntuación del diálogo; dictado de 3 oraciones diarias.
  • Escritura con "estructura" en 0-1: planificar con tres cajas antes de escribir, siempre; escribir un texto corto por semana y revisarlo juntos con la rúbrica.
  • Speaking con "corrección" en 0-1: grabar 2 minutos de habla, escucharlo juntos y que el niño detecte sus propios errores de tiempo verbal.
  • Si todo está sobre 80%: el siguiente nivel es Common Core Grade 6 y Cambridge B1 Preliminary for Schools; ya no tiene sentido evaluarlo como aprendiz de inglés.
